title: A Far-Right ‘Constitutional Sheriff’ Departs, but His Legacy May Endure
author: Jacob Jones
content:
_This story is produced as a collaboration between Bolts
and[InvestigateWest](https://investigatewest.org/)_,_an independent news
nonprofit dedicated to investigative journalism in the Pacific Northwest_. _It
is_ _part of Bolts ' series on sheriff races_ _this fall; read our coverage
from[Maryland](https://boltsmag.org/frederick-county-immigration-enforcement-
sheriff-chuck-jenkins/), [North Carolina](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-
county-sheriff-terry-johnson-shannon-long/), and
[Wisconsin](https://boltsmag.org/wisconsin-sheriff-races-immigration-sauk-
winnebago/)._

  
Beneath a wide-brimmed, black cowboy hat, Klickitat County Sheriff Bob Songer
warned in a Facebook video earlier this year that state lawmakers planned to
strip voters of the freedom to elect their own local leaders.

“They’ll decide who qualifies to run for sheriff,” Songer said of the
Democrats running Washington’s state Legislature. “If the sheriff is not
toeing the governor’s mandates … then they remove the sheriff.”

An American flag hung on the wall behind him as he recorded his “call to
action” from his office in the rural county along the Columbia River in
southern Washington state. He encouraged citizens to oppose the new
legislation that would set minimum qualifications for county sheriffs,
regulate department volunteers and allow for the removal of sheriffs who lose
their peace officer certifications.

The legislation was a response, in part, to “constitutional sheriffs” like
Songer who reject the state’s authority over them and say they get to decide
what laws are unconstitutional. Songer cast it as an attack on Klickitat
County’s residents. “They’re violating your rights,” he said.

Songer, 81, has drawn national attention as an outspoken figure of the
constitutional sheriff movement, which civil rights watchdogs describe as a
far-right, anti-government ideology that dangerously asserts elected local
sheriffs can nullify state or federal law. He has championed the sovereign
authority of sheriffs across the country, linking up with [like-
minded](https://www.splcenter.org/resources/extremist-files/constitutional-
sheriffs/) lawmen.

At home, he has rejected the state’s authority to tell him how to uphold the
law in Klickitat County. He has defied gun control measures and COVID-19
public health mandates, recruited an [armed
posse](https://www.investigatewest.org/in-a-rural-stretch-of-washington-a-
constitutional-sheriff-and-his-growing-volunteer-posse-provoke-controversy/)
of more than 100 volunteers and asked immigration agents to [put him on “speed
dial”](https://www.investigatewest.org/most-wa-sheriffs-say-they-will-follow-
states-sanctuary-law-with-a-few-exceptions/)—despite a state law prohibiting
cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. His aggressive posturing has
split his community into devout supporters against outraged critics.

With Songer retiring this year, many voters seem eager to turn the page. The
candidate Songer supported as his successor, Detective Sgt. Tony Warren, a
Republican, received just 27 percent of the vote in the all-party primary in
August, far behind former deputy Dwayne Matulovich, who is running as an
independent and received 57 percent. Matulovich and Warren must face off again
next month in a two-person runoff.

In the campaign, Warren has echoed Songer’s claim that sheriffs have the
authority to not enforce laws they think are unconstitutional. That claim is
core to the constitutional sheriff’s movement, and is one Matulovich has
distanced himself from.

But both men also sounded similar notes in interviews with _Bolts_ and
_InvestigateWest_ , signaling that some of Songer’s legacy is bound to endure
no matter who wins in November. Both candidates said they respected Songer’s
dedication to constitutional freedoms, but want to keep their priorities
anchored in the county’s local challenges and community safety. And both were
broadly supportive of one of the more [controversial aspects of Songer’s
tenure](https://www.investigatewest.org/in-a-rural-stretch-of-washington-a-
constitutional-sheriff-and-his-growing-volunteer-posse-provoke-
controversy/)—his use of volunteer posses that operate under his direction
with few guidelines.

Across the country, other sheriffs who align with far-right organizations are
[also facing](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-
shannon-long/) [significant pushback](https://boltsmag.org/frederick-county-
immigration-enforcement-sheriff-chuck-jenkins/) [this
fall,](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-county-sheriff-terry-johnson-shannon-
long/) often from [immigrant communities](https://boltsmag.org/alamance-
county-sheriff-terry-johnson-shannon-long/) that have been targeted by local
law enforcement, though candidates challenging them often sound a cautious
note.

Washington lawmakers in March ended up passing the legislation Songer warned
about in his “call to action,” joining other states in adopting qualification
standards for sheriffs and limiting the uses of volunteer posses. State
Representative Roger Goodman, a Democrat and chair of the House Community
Safety Committee, said he backed these reforms in part due to concerns he
heard directly from Klickitat County residents about potential abuses of
authority.

“Constitutional sheriffs believe that they interpret the Constitution,”
Goodman said. “They enforce the law as they interpret it. [But] in practice,
it ends up being a failure to enforce the wildlife laws, women’s reproductive
freedom, the laws to make sure our elections are truly nonpartisan and safe,
the laws related to firearms safety.”

“We establish a duty of the sheriff to enforce the law,” he added, “which is
kind of absurd to have to put into the law.”

* * *

Much of the modern constitutional sheriff movement [has coalesced
around](https://azcir.org/news/2023/08/21/constitutional-counties-adopt-
constitutional-sheriff-ideology/) the Constitutional Sheriffs and Peace
Officers Association founded in 2011 by Richard Mack, a former sheriff of
Graham County, Arizona. The Southern Poverty Law Center[ described the
CSPOA](https://www.splcenter.org/resources/extremist-files/constitutional-
sheriffs/#top-takeaways) as an “extremist group” with ideological roots in
antigovernment and sovereign citizen movements. The Anti-Defamation League[
reports](https://www.adl.org/resources/report/constitutional-sheriffs-and-
peace-officers-association-cspoa-and-richard-mack-how) Mack has used the CSPOA
to push conspiracy theories and far-right propaganda.

Songer is a CSPOA board member and he has talked at CSPOA conferences that
have convened sheriffs from around the country.

Mirya Holman, a professor at the Hobby School of Public Affairs at the
University of Houston, said the association claims that elected sheriffs have
unique authority granted by the voters to enforce laws at their discretion in
order to protect constitutional rights. She explained they regularly recite
false legal doctrines as justification.

“None of it is legally true,” she said. “There’s no legal grounding for that.
That doesn’t exist.”

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Songerportrait.jpg)Klickitat County Sheriff Bob
Songer, here shown in his office in Goldendale in 2023, is not running for
reelection this year (photo by Isaac Stone Simonelli for Arizona Center for
Investigative Reporting).

In researching her book “[The Power of the
Badge](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/P/bo220537347.html)”
with co-author Emily Farris, Holman said she found the movement had leveraged
grievances on gun control, COVID-19, wildlife conflicts, immigration, federal
overreach and election security to gain ground with voters—particularly in
Western states and other rural areas, including Klickitat County.

But despite the accountability to the voters that constitutional sheriffs
often cite as the ultimate safeguard, Holman said many sheriffs[ run term
after term unopposed](https://www.governing.com/magazine/uncontested-the-
surprising-political-invulnerability-of-sheriffs), or they can expect to run
against someone who previously worked for them.

“It turns out that when you are the boss of all of your future political
opponents … you could make sure that people that are potential political
competitors don't receive leadership roles or don't receive the training that
would help them,” she said. “You can engage in retaliation against people that
you think are going to run against you.”

Both candidates hoping to succeed Songer have worked under him.

Warren, a current detective sergeant for the county, and Matulovich, a
longtime law enforcement officer who left the sheriff’s office in 2023, both
told _Bolts_ and _InvestigateWest_ they wanted to move the department away
from national culture wars so they could focus on local outreach and day-to-
day improvements to service.

“A lot of people would have rather had Songer’s attention here,” Matulovich
said. “[The national constitutional sheriff movement] was his passion, so
that’s fine, but I think it kind of took away from things here within the
county. … To me, it felt like it divided the county a little bit.”

When asked about cooperating with immigration enforcement, both Warren and
Matulovich said they would not task deputies to work with federal agencies.

“If they're going to come to these communities and they want to do
enforcement, that's on them,” Warren said. “If it escalates or additional
crimes are broken … we'll take enforcement action on the local end. But I'm
not going to ask people to go out and work side by side with immigration
enforcement.”

Another point of contention has been Flock Safety cameras and other automated
license plate readers that have [drawn public
outrage](https://boltsmag.org/jefferson-county-florida-rural-sheriff-
dismantles-flock-camera-network/) over privacy concerns and police abuses.
While Warren previously described the cameras as a valuable investigative
tool, both candidates now say they oppose investing in the cameras over
privacy, budget and public record considerations.

“It’s overly abused,” Matulovich said. “The public records [requests] would be
a nightmare and we’re too small of a department to keep up with those, so I
would not be in favor of Flock cameras in our county.”

Both candidates have tried to walk a fine line on their relationship to
Songer.

Matulovich has said he disagrees with the view constitutional sheriffs espouse
that their office has direct authority to enforce and interpret the
Constitution. He told a July 21 candidate forum that he would leave legal
interpretation up to the courts.

“The fight is [on] the judicial side,” he said. “On the executive branch,
where discretion is allowed, I will use it wisely.”

But Matulovich also said he shares Songer’s commitment to protecting
individual rights, mostly disagreeing on the sheriff’s implementation of those
values: “It was almost like too much of a good thing became bad.”

Financial disclosures show Songer has donated to Warren’s campaign. But Warren
rejects characterizations that he would serve as a “Bob [Songer] 2.0”and said
he “can appreciate the concerns for [CSPOA] being an extremist group and the
concerns that CSPOA members are putting themselves above the law.”

But he also warned state officials would “trample on your rights in a
heartbeat,” and criticized some state bills as “ridiculous” during the July 21
forum.

“I have no issue not enforcing those things,” Warren told the crowd. “Whether
it’s mask mandates, blatant firearm restrictions, we see this state pass bills
that get overturned in other states and it’s just absurd.”

An enthusiastic applause filled the room.

* * *

When running for his first term as Klickitat County Sheriff in 2014, Songer
promised to start up a[ volunteer posse](https://www.investigatewest.org/in-a-
rural-stretch-of-washington-a-constitutional-sheriff-and-his-growing-
volunteer-posse-provoke-controversy/) to increase community involvement with
the department. In the years since, he has dispatched dozens of volunteer
posse members to front desk duty, event security, search-and-rescue efforts
and other tasks. At times, Songer has also authorized certain armed posse
members to engage in [controversial cougar hunts](https://www.nwpb.org/nw-
news/2022-01-19/washington-bill-aims-to-stop-controversial-cougar-hunts-in-
klickitat-county) or act as courtroom security.

Supporters of the posse have cast the volunteers as essential manpower for a
budget-strapped county, but others argue posse members should not wear
uniforms that resemble certified law enforcement or carry firearms. Gabrielle
Gilbert, a Klickitat community advocate and longtime Songer critic, said the
sheriff would seemingly wield the posse like a personal militia to scare off
outside interference.

“If anybody came for anyone based on a law that he didn’t agree with, he would
deputize a room full of people,” she said. “Those were the kind of threats
that you were under.”

Goodman, the state lawmaker, said Washington previously lacked regulations
around how sheriffs could deploy volunteers. As the state worked to reform
police accountability standards in the wake of George Floyd’s death, Goodman
said it seemed increasingly important to set standards for sheriff
qualifications and what duties require peace officer certification—based in
part on posse complaints from Klickitat County.

“We received from that area a lot of serious concern about untrained
volunteers wielding weapons, going on people’s property, hunting cougars with
dogs … and doing a lot of other things,” he said.

Goodman worked with Democratic state Sen. John Lovick, a former Snohomish
County Sheriff and state trooper of 31 years, to pass[ Senate Bill
5974](https://app.leg.wa.gov/BillSummary/?BillNumber=5974&Year=2025&Initiative=false)
during the 2026 legislative session. The bill sets minimum age, criminal
history and experience criteria for sheriff candidates. It also outlined a
process for removing sheriffs if a state commission revoked their peace
officer certification.

Many Washington sheriffs joined Songer in attacking the bill. In a testimony
[perceived](https://www.thenewstribune.com/news/local/article314342053.html)
by many observers as threatening lawmakers, Pierce County Sheriff Keith Swank
said it would give “unelected bureaucracy the ability to decertify me and
remove me from office because you don’t agree with my speech.” Swank [faces a
ballot measure this fall](https://boltsmag.org/pierce-county-sheriff-
elections-or-appointments/) that’d remove him from office.

“To be clear, no one is decertified for being unpopular,” Lovick responded in
a[ statement](https://senatedemocrats.wa.gov/lovick/2026/04/01/bill-to-
improve-public-safety-by-strengthening-eligibility-and-professional-standards-
for-law-enforcement-leaders-signed-by-governor/) this spring. “It is an
apolitical process guided by the clear and objective conduct standards
followed by every other officer in our state.”

The League of Women Voters of Washington, Disability Rights Washington, the
Northwest Immigrant Rights Projects and other organizations representing
vulnerable communities voiced strong support for the law in public hearings.

“Other states already do this,” testified Kristin Ang of the Faith Action
Network, citing legally established sheriff qualifications and removal
standards in California, Colorado, Georgia, Kansas, Massachusetts and Texas.
“Serious misconduct is no less serious because the person who committed it is
a sheriff.”

Four county sheriffs and the Washington State Sheriffs’ Association filed
separate lawsuits challenging the new legislation. A Thurston County Superior
Court judge on Oct. 2 struck down the new eligibility and removal standards,
though The Washington State Standard, an online news outlet,
[reported](https://washingtonstatestandard.com/2026/10/02/judge-permanently-
blocks-wa-sheriff-standards-law/) that the ruling did not appear to block the
other new laws on law enforcement volunteers. The state plans to appeal the
ruling.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/gym-sign_ISS.jpg)Songer
pushed for a resolution declaring Klickitat County a so-called constitutional
county; here a sign supporting the proposal rests in the window of a
storefront in Goldendale in July 2023 (photo by Isaac Stone Simonelli for
Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting).

Matulovich and Warren both praised Songer’s efforts to develop volunteer
support for the small sheriff’s office. Both acknowledged the posse program
needed changes—whether forced by state law or not—but showed no intention of
ending it. They planned to introduce new attire that does not look like a law
enforcement uniform along with developing more distinction between trained
reserve deputy duties and volunteer posse assignments.

“It’s great to have volunteers,” Matulovich said. “Volunteers are the backbone
of small agencies … [but] the posse would be support for like a lot of the
things they do for parades, for rodeos, for events. They would be there for
support, but they're not going to be there for armed security.”

Warren said calling volunteers a “posse” may be part of the problem, but he
wants to continue using volunteers for traffic control, evacuations,
observations and administrative tasks. He hopes that public outreach, training
and different uniforms can help clarify what volunteers can and should do.

He said remained open to a “select few” armed volunteers such as retired law
enforcement or specially trained courtroom security.

“They need to be trained,” Warren said, “and they need to be capable.”

* * *

In response to Songer’s “call to action” video on Facebook, hundreds of
people—including many from far outside Klickitat County—posted messages of
support. They thanked Songer for standing strong and defending freedom. Some
suggested he arrest state officials. Others alleged Democrats had rigged
elections to ensure their majority power.

But there’s been plenty of opposition to Songer, too.

Songer won his last reelection race in 2022 by just 150 votes, beating a
fellow Republican [who said](https://www.goldendalesentinel.com/garique-
clifford/article_f74b9868-2958-11ed-9ea9-abed2ae75fbc.html) the incumbent was
too “combative.”

Gilbert, the local advocate, said plenty of people still support Songer, but
many residents want to move past the bluster, intimidation and distrust of his
administration.

“People are tired,” she said. “They’re tired of the status quo. They’re tired
of being in the press nationally … for all the wrong reasons.”

She added that she hopes the election will restore a culture of competency at
the Klickitat County Sheriff’s Office. Public servants, she said, should be
working for “solutions and not for a soundbite.”
